edits.old: Six other Halomonas genomes also contained multiple MPn transport and degradation genes, while 17 did not (Figure 5).
edits.new: In GTDB release R232, which divides the former genus *Halomonas* among *Halomonas*, *Vreelandella*, and several smaller genera, both isolates remain in *Halomonas*: *H. saccharevitans* shares 98.5% average nucleotide identity (ANI) with the type strain genome, and *Halomonas* sp. D is the representative of its own species cluster (*Halomonas* sp032334135; closest other species, 92.7% ANI). Six other reference genomes labeled *Halomonas* also contained multiple MPn transport and degradation genes, while 17 did not (Figure 5); in GTDB R232, three of these six (*Halomonas* sp. PBN3, *H. huangheensis*, and *Halomonas* sp. S2151) remain in *Halomonas*, whereas *H. jeotgali* is now placed in *Vreelandella* and *H. zincidurans* and *H. lutea* in *Modicisalibacter*.
edits.rationale: Reports the isolates' R232 placement (review comment 3). The six/17 counts still describe the Figure 5 labels, but three of the six MPn-positive 'Halomonas' references are in other genera in R232. All six are resolved unambiguously by strain, so this sentence does not depend on the H. campaniensis inference. I1's GTDB match is to its own deposited genome, so it is described as its own species cluster, not as a 100% ANI identification.

edits.old: only Halomonas contains members with the genes encoding the C-P lyase pathway
edits.new: This is a genus-level statement based on reference genomes (Figure 5). In the metagenome, neither Halomonadaceae MAG carries C–P lyase genes (phnF–P, including phnJ): Halomonas.1 (H. fontilapidosi) and 2020 Halomonas.2 (now Vreelandella.1 in R232). Neither isolate matches any of the 450 MAGs at species level (skani: best pair I4 vs Halomonas.1, 85.7% ANI over ~25% of the genome). The C-P lyase Halomonas is therefore supported by the isolate, not by the MAGs; consider saying so where Halomonas is presented as the case study (the Culturing discussion and the Conclusions).

edits.old: These findings were corroborated by metabolic modeling, whereby the trace consumption of methylphosphonic acid reproduced the experimentally measured methane emissions, providing further evidence for methylphosphonate being a primary methanogenic substrate in these saltern environments.
edits.new: Metabolic modeling showed that trace consumption of methylphosphonic acid by the methylphosphonate-consuming community members could supply about half of the measured methane emissions, consistent with methylphosphonate being an important methanogenic substrate in these saltern environments, although the simulated emissions did not track the differences among cores.
edits.rationale: On the consistent areal basis the MPn models give 56% of the measured total (18–141% by core) but Spearman ρ = −0.20 (exact p = 0.71, n = 6). The stored fluxes were simulated with each model's biomass fixed to the mean over depths of relative abundance divided by DNA. Two depths have almost no DNA (R2_B_D1 and R2_C_D2, 0.16 µg g−1 soil), so that input carries a 1/DNA term, which multiplying by the core's DNA does not cancel. Both the draft's fits (R² 0.978/0.968/0.862, both axes divided by DNA) and an intermediate 'areal' correction (ρ = 0.60) came from that term: the factor VW_DNA × mean(1/DNA) alone has ρ = 0.60 against measured methane. On the consistent basis used here, each MAG's flux per unit of simulated abundance (a constant for every MePn model) is rescaled to its biomass in the core (relative abundance × DNA × layer thickness).

edits.old: requiring substantially more adjustments in the slope and th
edits.new: which has a negative slope; the simulated betaine-derived methane exceeded the measured emissions in five of the six cores. In the reported solution, four of the nine betaine reducers (UBA8670.2 of the Dethiosulfatibacteraceae, DATFJG01.1 of the Acidaminobacteraceae, BM714.2, and M55B127.2) consumed betaine at the uptake bound, and so produced the maximum methane allowed, in all six cores; *Halanaerobium*.2 was forced to excrete no TMA, and for several other models (including *Halanaerobium*.1 and BM714.4) the TMA excretion was not unique, zero being one of many equally optimal solutions. Because 33 of the 54 simulated betaine fluxes were at the uptake bound, the summed TMA excretion varied only 1.3-fold among cores, while the DNA-normalized abundance that fixed the model biomass varied 14.5-fold, so the simulated betaine-derived methane followed the soil DNA density used in the unit conversion (R^2^ = 0.97) rather than the abundance of betaine reducers; this comparison is therefore not a strong test of the betaine hypothesis.
edits.rationale: Nine grdH carriers: model/measured 0.83 (R2_C) to 5.47 (R1_A), so >1 in five cores. FVA at the lactate optimum: Halanaerobium.2 forced to 0; Halanaerobium.1 FVA minimum 0 in every core (non-unique), BM714.4 non-unique; UBA8670.2, DATFJG01.1, BM714.2, M55B127.2 at 0.1 in all six cores in the stored solution. 33 of 54 cells at the bound; summed TMA 1.32-fold vs 14.5-fold in the model-input (DNA-normalized) abundance; simulated betaine methane vs VW DNA R² 0.973.

edits.old: The models further reveal that methane is produced stoichiometrically from betaine and almost from methylphosphonate (1.4 methane : 1 methylphosphonate).
edits.new: In the models, each methylphosphonate consumed yields exactly one methane (1 methane : 1 methylphosphonate), whereas methane from betaine was set by assumption to 0.06 of the TMA excreted (Methods).
edits.rationale: CH4/MePn is 1.000 for every MAG and core in saltern_fluxes.json at 0.07 and 0.33, in every committed version (c49e503, a725dce, 1b758a4) and in the substrate-addition run. The 1.4 is not supported. Betaine CH4 = 0.06 × TMA is the Methods assumption (P36), not a model result.

edits.old: This was mechanistically corroborated by metabolic models that reproduced the experimental methane emissions with high accuracy (R2 = 0.978), and demonstrate that methane is generated stoichiometrically from methylphosphonate.
edits.new: Metabolic models of the MPn consumers produced methane at rates of the same order as the experimental emissions in the unrestored cores (about half in total at a phosphate source ratio of 0.07), with one methane generated per methylphosphonate consumed, but neither these models nor the betaine models tracked the differences in emissions among the six cores (Spearman ρ = −0.20 and −0.09).
edits.rationale: 0.978 is fits.json[0.07] (both axes divided by DNA). Consistent basis: MPn 56% of measured, ρ −0.20; betaine ρ −0.09. CH4:MePn = 1.000 in every MAG and core.

edits.old: The high average correlation of all members is attributed to higher metabolic activity of community members when in the regime of producing methane.
edits.rationale: Contradicts the revised Results, which attribute the community-wide correlation with methane to the separation of the high-methane unrestored salterns from the other sites (254 of 310 MAGs correlated; no guild beats random sets on the areal basis).

edits.old: The metabolic models only parameterized the relative abundances of each member and trace consumption of methylphosphonate, which encourages that these are natural outcomes of the metabolism and not forced behaviors during optimization.
edits.new: The metabolic models only parameterized the relative abundances of each member and a minimum ratio of methylphosphonate to inorganic phosphate uptake. Because the simulated methane of each member is then proportional to its abundance, the models mainly translate the abundance of MPn consumers into methane; that the ratio constraint did not bind for three Rhodobacteraceae models suggests that, for these organisms, methylphosphonate consumption is a natural outcome of their metabolism rather than a forced behavior.
edits.rationale: Modelled CH4 per unit of model-input abundance is one of three constants per MAG (0.04321, 0.46974, 0.55344 at 0.07; CV ≤ 1e-9). The constraint binds in 17 of 20 models.

edits.new: Thirdly, metabolic models showed that trace consumption of methylphosphonate, with one methane per methylphosphonate consumed, can account for about half of the methane emitted from the unrestored salterns, although the simulated emissions did not track the differences among cores. edits.rationale: Consistent basis at 0.07: 56% in total (18–141% by core; two cores above 1), ρ −0.20.

edits.old: We therefore propose methylphosphonate as the primary source of methane
edits.new: Consider hedging this conclusion. The modeling now shows that methylphosphonate consumption can supply methane of the measured magnitude but not the pattern among cores (Figure 7), and guild abundance tracks methane more specifically for MPn consumers only on the DNA-normalized basis (Table 5). The strongest support is the substrate-addition (Figure 4) and culturing (Figure 6) evidence. For example: 'We therefore propose methylphosphonate as the most consistent candidate source of methane…'.
edits.rationale: The Conclusions keep unqualified claims ('primary source', 'precise mechanism') that the revised Results no longer support.

edits.old: Figure 7. Assessing methylphosphonate and betaine metabolism
edits.new: Figure 7. Simulated versus measured methane emissions in the six unrestored cores. Orange: summed methane flux of the 20 simulated methylphosphonate-consuming models (phosphate source ratio 0.07), each rescaled to the member’s biomass in the core (relative abundance × soil DNA density of each depth, weighted by depth). Blue: summed methane of the nine betaine-reducing models (MAGs carrying *grdH*; methane = 0.06 × TMA excretion), converted with the core’s volume-weighted DNA density because their TMA excretion was mostly set by the uptake bound. Both axes are in µmol CH~4~ m^−2^ d^−1^ on log scales; the dotted line marks 1:1 agreement and the dashed lines are linear fits. Methylphosphonate-derived methane is of the same order as the measured emissions (56% of the total; 18–141% among cores) but does not track them (Spearman ρ = −0.20, exact p = 0.71; R^2^ = 0.08); betaine-derived methane does not track them either (ρ = −0.09, p = 0.92; R^2^ = 0.10). Guild abundance versus methane is shown in Figure 9 and Table 5.
edits.rationale: Single panel on the consistent basis (clauded_insights/figure7_r232.png); the old panel b (abundance vs methane) is superseded by Figure 9, Figure S8 and Table 5. The stored fluxes were simulated with each model's biomass fixed to the mean over depths of relative abundance divided by DNA. Two depths have almost no DNA (R2_B_D1 and R2_C_D2, 0.16 µg g−1 soil), so that input carries a 1/DNA term, which multiplying by the core's DNA does not cancel. Both the draft's fits (R² 0.978/0.968/0.862, both axes divided by DNA) and an intermediate 'areal' correction (ρ = 0.60) came from that term: the factor VW_DNA × mean(1/DNA) alone has ρ = 0.60 against measured methane. On the consistent basis used here, each MAG's flux per unit of simulated abundance (a constant for every MePn model) is rescaled to its biomass in the core (relative abundance × DNA × layer thickness).
